Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette: The typhoon had struck on a humid Tuesday, transforming the coastal district into a churning flood of debris and rising water. Minh had been stranded on the fourth floor of a commercial complex when the surge breached the ground level. He remembered the shocking cold of the water lapping against his ankles, the sudden groan of buckling concrete, and the metallic, coppery taste of rust and rainwater flooding his mouth as he hauled himself onto a rusted service ladder. His neck had seized from the unnatural angle he held while clinging to the rungs, a sharp, grinding pain that never truly left him. He waited for hours, watching emergency boats drift past without stopping. By the time rescue arrived, the exhaustion had curdled into a deep, nausea-inducing dread that settled in his stomach and refused to lift. In the weeks that followed, the calm was a lie. It began with the weather alerts on his phone. Whenever the barometric pressure dropped or the sky bruised purple, a familiar ache would bloom at the base of his skull, tight and unyielding. That physical warning was never long before the flood returned. The moment his neck stiffened, the memory would hijack his mind, dragging him back to that ladder with such intensity that he would drop whatever he was holding. He would sit there, certain that the account felt so extreme it was hard to believe it had actually happened to him, yet the taste of copper and rot would flood his tongue with impossible clarity. Without a coherent image forming, the sheer terror of those hours would crash over him, completely unbidden. Once the memory took hold, his understanding of the world fractured in a way he could not control. He found himself convinced that the people who had not stopped, the neighbors who had moved on, and the emergency services that had bypassed him were fundamentally untrustworthy. The terror of being left behind hardened into a quiet certainty that he was separated from the rest of the world, a permanent exile in his own city. When he sat in the glass-walled conference rooms at his UX design firm, mapping user journeys and testing interface flows, he felt completely untethered, as though the language of human connection was spoken by others while he remained isolated on the outside. That conviction did not sit quietly. Because he was certain that others could not be relied upon, his attention snapped to every potential sign of danger. Routine shifts in the weather or even a colleague’s offhand comment about an approaching front would instantly flare that initial neck tension, rewiring his nervous system before he could consciously process what was happening. The appraisal that people were fundamentally unreliable became a lens that magnified every trigger, turning ordinary atmospheric changes into imminent threats that demanded his immediate vigilance. This reinforcement only tightened with time. At the office, a sudden gust of wind rattling the high-rise windows, the sound of heavy rain drumming against the glass, or even a project manager’s urgent tone about a deadline would instantly push him toward the same conclusion: he belonged nowhere, and no one was truly looking out for him. The triggers did not just spark the past; they actively poisoned his present relationships and professional focus. He stopped attending team lunches, declining invitations with quiet excuses, because the weight of that isolation felt heavier than the discomfort of staying behind. Even when he tried to ground himself, the memories would bleed back through the cracks. The emotion without a clear image would surface during routine tasks, a sudden, nameless dread that would immediately trigger the familiar somatic warning and hypervigilance, turning ordinary moments into potential threats. As that emotion spiked, the physical tension in his neck would lock further, making him flinch at sudden movements or loud noises, which in turn forced the intrusive memories to surface again. The cycle of dread and somatic alarm became his new normal, a silent architecture running beneath his days. He finally booked a session after a usability testing session derailed when a dropped stylus sounded like shattering glass. Sitting in his therapist’s office, he admitted he was exhausted from holding his breath through every passing storm, terrified that the ground would open up again. He wanted to stop bracing for a disaster that had already passed, hoping someone might help him untangle the knot before it pulled him completely under.
